name: Jamal Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Can we start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a firm that restores old buildings, churches, water mills, a few big timber barns. This month we're replacing rotten beams in a church roof that's about four hundred years old. A normal day, I'm up in the roof by eight with a torch, poking at oak with a screwdriver to see how deep the rot goes, then down at the workbench cutting new joints to match the old ones. It's slow work and I love it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that every joint tells you who cut it. You can see where some carpenter centuries ago made a mistake and fixed it, and I'm talking to him in a way. The hard part is the cold up in those roofs, and the paperwork for the heritage officers, they want a photo and a report for every peg. My partner Lucia's a dental hygienist and she says I come home smelling like a damp library.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. We scan the old roofs with a laser scanner, and I use an AI program to turn the scan into a 3D model and work out the cut list for new beams. I use the chat ones to write the heritage reports from my notes, which saves me hours. And at home I've got a CNC router in the garage, a computer-controlled cutting machine, and I make furniture on weekends that I sell online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a shame, but it's still a handy set of tools. At work I'd keep showing people how I use the scanner and the reports. Online I'd probably post a picture of a church beam and say, still needs a human, and get twelve likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's fine. I've got a few years left, good money, savings, and the furniture business on the side. I'd keep using what I use, and the slow, careful work I do doesn't change much anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at work, same jobs. I'd probably buy a bigger CNC bed for the garage, it's about four thousand, so I can make dining tables, not just side tables. And I'd keep growing the online shop slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit underwhelmed. I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the furniture side now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, maybe five or six thousand a year. Mostly oak side tables with old-style joints, people like that they're made by a real carpenter. I see it as my retirement job, something to keep my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the heritage officers say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be relieved, I think, some of them are nervous about computers touching old buildings. One of them, Margaret, still asks for printed photos. She'd be happy.

S0.say: It's a shame, but AI is still a handy set of tools. He'd post a church beam online with the line that it still needs a human.
S0.think: He's fine, with good money, savings and a furniture business on the side, and his slow, careful restoration work wouldn't change much anyway.
S0.do: Keeps working on the same jobs and buys a bigger CNC bed for his garage, about four thousand, to make dining tables. Grows his online furniture shop slowly.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit underwhelmed, because he likes new toys.
S0.quote: I'd probably post a picture of a church beam and say, still needs a human, and get twelve likes.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is an enthusiast whose restoration work and side business both stay secure here. He's mildly disappointed rather than relieved. His furniture shop is already a planned retirement job, which gives him a cushion beyond savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for people who learn it and tough for people who don't. At work I'd keep pushing the boss to use the scanning and modelling on every job. Online I'd post more videos of how I use the AI on old buildings, because people find that interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd do better. Restoration needs judgement, someone has to decide which beam to save and which to replace, and AI makes my planning faster. And the furniture side could grow, because the machines would make me quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get the firm to buy a robot arm for the workshop, they can cut complicated joints in a fraction of the time. I'd train two of the younger carpenters on the scanner and the modelling. At home I'd put more into the furniture, maybe hire a part-time helper for finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like a chance to do more of the interesting part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank, our oldest joiner. He's brilliant with a chisel and wants nothing to do with screens. I'd keep him on the hand finishing, because people still want to see real tool marks on old churches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the heritage officers accept robot-cut joints?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, some wouldn't. I'd use the robot to rough out the joint and then finish it by hand, so it looks right and it's honest. That's a compromise I can live with.

S1.say: This is good news for people who learn it and tough for those who don't. He'd push the boss to use scanning and modelling on every job and post videos about AI on old buildings.
S1.think: He'd do better, because restoration needs human judgement on which beams to save and AI speeds up his planning. His furniture business could grow too.
S1.do: Gets the firm to buy a robot arm for cutting joints in the workshop and trains two younger carpenters on scanning and modelling. Puts more into the furniture side and hires a part-time finishing helper.
S1.feel: Calm and excited about doing more of the interesting work.
S1.quote: I'd use the robot to rough out the joint and then finish it by hand, so it looks right and it's honest.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees steady change as an opportunity at work and at home. He's practical about keeping an old hand-tool joiner where his skills matter. His compromise on robot-cut joints shows he values honesty in the craft, not just speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and we need to be careful, especially on old buildings where mistakes can't be undone. At work I'd say we should be the firm that learns to use it properly, not the one that gets pushed aside. Online I'd be talking about it a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I'd be sixty and I could stop. We've got savings and the house is paid off. But I'd worry about the furniture business, because if a robot can make a dining table as well as me and cheaper, the online shop is dead. And my son Andre's a chef, so I'd worry about kitchens too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd push the firm to buy the robot systems and make me the person who runs them on restoration jobs, so I'm still useful. I'd change the furniture to one-off commissions, where people pay for the story, not the table. And I'd put a bit more into savings for a couple of years while I see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and worried in the same breath, which is a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the online shop could be dead. Would that bother you more than losing the main job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, which surprises me. The main job I'd be leaving soon anyway. The furniture was going to be what I did when I stopped, so it's my retirement I'd be losing, not my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Andre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him people still want to eat with someone who cares about the food. Robots can cook, fine, but a good restaurant is about the people. I'd tell him to keep his own place small and personal.

S2.say: This is huge and needs care, especially on old buildings where mistakes can't be undone. He'd want his firm to be the one that learns it properly, not the one pushed aside.
S2.think: At sixty with savings and a paid-off house he could stop, but the furniture shop he planned for retirement could be killed by cheaper robot-made tables. He also worries about his son's work as a chef.
S2.do: Pushes the firm to buy robot systems and puts himself in charge of running them on restoration jobs. Switches the furniture business to one-off commissions and saves a bit more for a couple of years.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and worried at once.
S2.quote: The furniture was going to be what I did when I stopped, so it's my retirement I'd be losing, not my work.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario surprises Jamal by threatening his planned retirement hobby more than his job. He still moves first, taking charge of the robots at work. His mood stays uneasy rather than anxious because his finances and adaptability give him room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it. At work I'd say let's train everyone now. Online I'd keep posting, probably about how restoration and robots can work together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually a good amount of time. I'd be sixty-three, ready to move into the furniture full time anyway. And I'd have five years to build a name, so people buy my pieces because they're mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two or three years getting the robot systems in at work and training the younger carpenters to run them. I'd put money into the furniture, a proper workshop, maybe fifteen thousand, and a website that tells the story of each piece. And I'd keep learning every new tool as it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit busy in my head, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen thousand is a big investment at that stage. Why risk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got the savings and I'd rather spend it on something I love than leave it sitting. If it fails, I've lost a workshop, not my house. Lucia's on board, she likes the idea of me out of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to leave behind at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three young carpenters who can scan an old roof, read the model and still cut a scarf joint by hand. That's the mix. If I leave that, I've done my job.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ahead of it, so train everyone now. He'd keep posting about how restoration and robots can work together.
S3.think: Five years suits him: at sixty-three he'd move into furniture full time and could build a name so people buy his pieces because they're his.
S3.do: Spends two or three years bringing robot systems into the firm and training younger carpenters to run them. Invests about fifteen thousand in a proper workshop and a website, and keeps learning each new tool.
S3.quote: If it fails, I've lost a workshop, not my house.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Jamal turns the threat into a plan to build a personal brand for his furniture. His risk-taking rests on solid savings and his partner's support. His legacy goal at the firm is a blend of digital and hand skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to get ready, so there's no excuse. I'd tell people to learn the tools now. I'd probably post about my own plans, because people like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's easy. I'd be sixty-eight, probably working in my workshop three days a week, making pieces people want for the story. The main job would be long done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire from the firm at about sixty-two, after getting the new tools settled in. Then I'd go full time on the furniture, maybe teach a weekend course on old joinery. I'd use whatever AI and robots help with the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd probably be looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach in a weekend course in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to cut a mortise and tenon by hand, with a chisel and mallet. People would come because they want to know how things used to be made. Maybe it'll be like pottery classes are now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'm not sure where young people will find their first jobs. I learned on a building site, carrying timber. If robots carry the timber, how does a sixteen-year-old get started?

S4.say: Ten years is a long time to get ready, so there's no excuse. He'd tell people to learn the tools now and post about his own plans.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he'd be making furniture three days a week, with people buying pieces for the story, and the main job long done.
S4.do: Retires from the firm at about sixty-two after settling in the new tools, then goes full time on furniture. Plans a weekend course on old joinery and uses AI and robots for the boring parts.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: If robots carry the timber, how does a sixteen-year-old get started?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Jamal is calm and planning a craft retirement with teaching on the side. His one real worry is how young people would get their first foot in the trade. He imagines hand joinery becoming a hobby skill, like pottery.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it could take the furniture business before I've even started properly, and young carpenters wouldn't get a chance to adjust. What would help is clear labelling, so people know what's made by a person and what's made by a machine, and support for apprenticeships so young people can still learn the trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the buildings. Old churches and mills were built by people, and when we repair them we're keeping that conversation going. I'd hate to see a robot do it so efficiently that we forget there was ever a person on the other end.

headlineQuote: You can see where some carpenter centuries ago made a mistake and fixed it, and I'm talking to him in a way.
portrait: Jamal Reyes is a 58-year-old lead carpenter at a firm that restores old churches, mills and barns, and he uses AI and laser scanning every day. He also runs a small online furniture business from a CNC workshop in his garage, which he sees as his retirement job. In every scenario he moves early, pushing his firm to adopt robots and training younger carpenters. The two-year AGI picture leaves him uneasy, mainly because it could kill the furniture business before he retires into it. With more time he'd invest in a proper workshop and a craft retirement with teaching on the side.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because it could take his furniture business before he's properly started and leave young carpenters no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Clear labelling of what's made by people versus machines, and support for apprenticeships so young people can still learn the trade.
